newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CLABECQ WINS STAY OF EXECUTION.
newsitem.headline: CLABECQ WINS STAY OF EXECUTION.

text.p: A Belgian commercial court has ruled against declaring Belgian steel maker Forges de Clabecq bankrupt and has instead appointed two experts to assess the company's chances of survival, a court spokesman said on Friday.

"Clabecq is not bankrupt...two experts have been appointed and they have to submit a first report to the court by Tuesday, December 24," the court official in the southern town of Nivelles told Reuters. He gave no further details.
Clabecq filed for bankruptcy on Thursday after its majority shareholder, Belgium's southern Walloon region, decided to withdraw its support.

About 1,000 Clabecq workers reacted on Friday by staging a violent demonstration through the centre of Clabecq's home town of Tubize, ransacking the local police office and smashing windows of bank offices, a Tubize fireman told Reuters.
One demonstrator was injured when a teargas grenade blew up in his face, he said.
"We have been cheated all along," one Clabecq worker told Belgian RTBF television.
The Belga news agency said its own reporter and photographer and several television cameramen had been pushed around by the angry crowd. It said phone booths had also been wrecked.
The demonstration was disbanded after a delegation met Tubize mayor -- and national parliament chairman -- Raymond Langendries.

Workers were also keeping the Clabecq plant occupied and denied access to the two court-named experts, one of whom is the company's general director William Smith, an American appointed to the job in October, Belgian radio said.

The fate of the loss-making steel firm, which employs more than 1,700 people, appeared to have been sealed on Wednesday when the European Commission rejected a rescue plan by the Walloon region for Clabecq.

The project involved an offer of 1.5 billion francs ($46.7 million) of capital, 700 million francs of credit, which had already granted, the writing-off of debts worth more than 800 million francs and the rescheduling of other borrowings.
The Commission said the subsidies went against EU rules which only allow steel sector aid for environmental reasons, for research and development or for company closure.
Walloon government Minister-President Robert Collignon said the government reserved the right to appeal against the Commission's decision to reject its rescue plan.
Collignon hopes that a certain amount of activity could be preserved at Clabecq, notably the blast furnace to supply the small nearby privately-owned steel firm Usines Gustave Boel.
The Brussels bourse on Friday said Clabecq shares would remain suspended until the court's final decision on whether to declare the company bankrupt.
"We'll wait for the final decision of the court. In the meantime, Clabecq remains suspended," a bourse official said.
"If the court had decided to declare Clabecq bankrupt, we would immediately have delisted it."
Clabecq shares closed down seven francs at 76 on Thursday,
A report on Clabecq commissioned by the Walloon region earlier this year showed its costs were 20 to 30 percent above the average of its competitors.
